text: The first spam email was sent in 1978. And it worked.
say: The first spam email was sent in nineteen seventy eight. And it worked.

text: Back then, the internet was ARPANET. A US government network linking universities and labs.
say: Back then, the internet was ARPANET. A U.S. government network linking universities and labs.

text: Only a few thousand people were on it, and email was for work. Nobody sent ads.
Then a marketer at a computer company called DEC had an idea.
say: Then a marketer at a computer company called Dec had an idea.

text: DEC was showing off its new computers in California, and he wanted every user on the West Coast to know.
say: Dec was showing off its new computers in California, and he wanted every user on the West Coast to know.

text: So instead of one email at a time, he sent the same invite to hundreds of people at once.
The replies were furious. One person said the message shut down his system.
The network's administrators told him off, and told him never to do it again.
But he later said it still paid off for the company.
Years later, people named this kind of email after a Monty Python sketch. Spam.
The lesson? Email still works. But only to people who said yes.
In Australia, it's the law. Get consent, say who you are, and add a working unsubscribe link.
